newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower after poor refunding.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower after poor refunding.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries slumped on Wednesday with the long bond down almost a full point after the government's quarterly refunding effort concluded with a poor result in its 10-year note auction, analysts said.

"The market was geared up for a lousy result, but if anything, it exceeded the market's expectations on the downside," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
"We cleared two auctions, both of which were lousy," said Karydakis.

Treasury prices were mostly weaker going into the auction, weighed down by a sagging dollar and disappointment over first-quarter U.S. productivity data. But the market took a bit more punishment after the sale.

With the average yield for the new 10-year coming in at 6.74 percent, the upper end of expectations, and the high bid awarded at a hefty 1.9 basis points over the average rate, experts said the auction was even sloppier than expected.
The bid to cover ratio was a relatively low 1.86 to one and non-competitive bids were a paltry $383 million.
The outstanding 10-year note ended down 20/32 at 96-13/32 to yield 6.76 percent. The benchmark 30-year bond was off 29/32 at 95-24/32, yielding 6.96 percent.
The auction largely overshawdowed the release of the Federal Reserve's Beige Book study of economic activity across the country.

The Fed's findings showed the U.S. economy expanded moderately in the last two months, with wages and retail prices remaining generally subdued. But the Fed also said labor markets remain tight, with qualified workers in demand across the country.
The report largely confirmed the picture of a fairly healthy economy painted by data in recent weeks, analysts said.
"I don't think it is going to change perceptions dramatically," Karydakis said. "I don't think the market is going to go down hard either. The rest of the week's economic calendar is pretty clear."

Earlier, the Labor Department reported that nonfarm productivity in the first quarter rose 2.0 percent, the biggest gain since the last quarter of 1993, but still below forecasts of a 2.4 percent gain.

Given speculation that the Fed may be concerned enough about tight labor conditions to raise rates again this month, the market was also somewhat alarmed by a 2.7 percent rise in unit labor costs, which were expected to be up only 1.0 percent.

"The productivity data came in a little weaker than expected. With a little bit higher labor costs embedded in that productivity data, that contributed to a slightly negative tone," said Brian Fabbri, chief economist at Paribas Capital Markets.
Analysts said the market seems divided over the prospects for a Fed rate hike at its May 20 policy setting meeting.

But First Chicago's Karydakis said the front end of the maturity curve is in the process of pricing in a rate hike, noting that the two-year note yield had risen more than 10 basis points over the last two sessions.
The two-year closed at 100-1/32, down 4/32, with a yield of 6.36 percent.
Also damaging market sentiment on Wednesday was a drop in the dollar, fueled by rumors that Japan, the United States and Germany were considering selling the U.S. unit to check its recent rally.
"That basically spooked the market early on ... because if the U.S. and Japan intervene against further dollar appreciation, it may cause Japanese investors to stop buying treasuries," Fabbri said.
Elsewhere, the five-year note was down 11/32 at 99-30/32 yielding 6.64 percent.
In the bill market, threes were at 5.10 percent, up five basis points. But the yield on six month bills fell one basis point to 5.34 percent due to technical factors, dealers said.
